title: Tilly and Pipkin Float Away
markdown:
It was a beautiful morning, and the world was just waking up. The sky was soft pink and sleepy orange. The sleepy stars were starting to yawn and go away. In a cozy hollow, beside a brook that sang a soft sleepy song, lived a little tabby kitten named Tilly. Tilly had stripes like toasted marmalade. Her tail twitched with every little thought, like a happy little thing. She loved her home and her friends. Her very best friend was Ned the duck. Ned was a plump fluffy ball. He gave sleepy sighs, and his feathers were white like snow. His nuzzle was always warm and comforting.

Tilly loved one thing best of all, and that was her little toy boat, Pipkin. Pipkin was painted sky blue, and it had a tiny red flag that always stood up straight and proud. Tilly always kept Pipkin on a smooth grey stone right by the stream. She liked to think Pipkin enjoyed feeling the cool water and listening to the brook’s song.

But this morning, when Tilly stretched her little paws and yawned a big kitten yawn, she looked at her special grey stone. Pipkin was not on the stone. Pipkin was on the stream.

A little shiver went through Tilly’s fur. Where could Pipkin be. She padded to the very edge of the water, her paws as light as dandelion fluff. And there, bobbing on the current, was Pipkin, floating away all by himself, heading towards the tall trees called the Whispering Willows. Now, the Whispering Willows were just tall trees with long green branches that swayed in the breeze. They were lovely, but at this early hour they looked big and far away.

Tilly looked at Pipkin, then at the trees. She really wanted Pipkin back before breakfast. She did not want to eat her yummy milk with a worried tummy. She looked around for Ned.

“Ned,” she whispered, her voice a little higher than usual.

Ned blinked one sleepy eye, then the other. “Mmmph,” he mumbled, his voice like a soft rustle of reeds. He often sounded like that when he was just waking up.

“Ned. Pipkin has floated away,” Tilly explained, her tail giving a little worried flick from side to side.

Ned tilted his head. “Floated away.” He blinked again. This time he saw Pipkin, a tiny blue speck, already drifting quite a way down the stream. “Oh, dear,” he said, his voice a little clearer. “We must get Pipkin back.”

Tilly knew they had to be quick. And she knew that Ned was her best friend, and even when he was sleepy, he was very good at helping.

“The stream goes past the Big Mossy Log,” Tilly said, her eyes following Pipkin’s path on the water. “Pipkin will go past there.”

“Hmm,” Ned said, waddling closer to the stream bank. “The Big Mossy Log is a bit wobbly. It has been there a long, long time.” He looked at Tilly, and even though his eyes were still a little droopy, they held a spark of quiet kindness. “But I know a way to cross it safely.”

And so, off they went. Tilly scampered ahead, her little paws light and quick over the soft grass, while Ned waddled steadily behind. They reached the Big Mossy Log. It was indeed quite mossy, and when Tilly tentatively put a paw on it, it wobbled just a tiny bit.

Tilly paused. Her ears flattened. She did not like wobbly things. What if I fall in, she thought. She imagined being all wet and mucky.

But here is the thing about Ned. He was often sleepy, but he was also very wise and kind. “Put your paws where my feet go,” he said softly. “I will go slow and steady. I will show you the best spots.”

Ned stepped carefully onto the log. Thump. Thump. His webbed feet found a good grip on the mossy surface. Tilly watched him, and then, taking a deep breath, she followed exactly where Ned’s feet had been. Tip-toe. Tip-toe. The log wobbled a little, but not too much, because Ned was being so careful. They made it safely to the other side, and Tilly purred a little thank you to Ned, rubbing against his soft feathers.

“Now,” Ned yawned, stretching his neck, “the stream bends here, you see. We have to go through the Tickly Reeds.” He pointed with his beak towards a tall green patch of reeds that rustled softly in the gentle morning breeze. Pipkin, the little blue boat, was indeed heading straight for them.

Tilly peered at the reeds. They looked tall and pokey. She imagined them tickling her nose and ears. What if they tickle too much and I cannot walk, she thought, her ears flattening just a little more.

Ned waddled right into the reeds. “The reeds might be tickly,” Ned said. “But they do not hurt. They are thin enough to push through.” He made a gentle path through the reeds with his beak, and Tilly followed, his soft quacks guiding her. The reeds brushed against her soft fur, and yes, they tickled. But they did not hurt at all. Soon they were through, and Pipkin was just a little bit further ahead.

They could see the Whispering Willows now, their branches drooping low like gentle sleepy arms reaching towards the water. And Pipkin. Pipkin was caught. A low branch, with long green ribbons, had snagged Pipkin’s little red flag. Pipkin could not float anymore, but he was too far for Tilly to reach from the bank.

Tilly looked at the branch. Pipkin was right there. Her heart went pitter-pat. “I have to get him,” she said, her voice small but firm.

Ned looked at the branch too, and then at brave little Tilly. He knew Tilly was small and nimble, perfect for reaching little things. “You are very brave, Tilly,” he said, his voice filled with quiet pride. “And I will help you get him.”

Tilly took a running start, her little legs pumping like tiny pistons. She leaped. The smell of damp earth filled her nose. The soft mud squished under her paws. The sight of Pipkin bobbing so close made her breath catch. With a final stretch, Tilly’s paw brushed Pipkin’s blue boat. She grabbed him with her claws. She pulled, and Pipkin wiggled free. He was safe in her paws.

Tilly hugged Pipkin close, purring. She was so happy. She looked back at Ned, who gave a slow contented blink. The sky was turning a beautiful soft gold now, and the sun was just peeking over the horizon, painting everything with warm light. They had done it. They had rescued Pipkin.

They hurried back, Pipkin held carefully in Tilly’s mouth. The Big Mossy Log seemed less wobbly now, and the Tickly Reeds just rustled a friendly greeting as they passed. Soon they were back at their cozy hollow.

“Pipkin,” Tilly said, and she gently set the little boat down on its special grey stone. He looked just as he should, his red flag standing tall and proud. Pipkin was not on the stream. Pipkin was on the stone.

Ned gave a happy soft quack. “You were very brave, Tilly. And you were very clever to follow my feet across the wobbly log.”

Tilly nuzzled Ned’s soft feathers. “And you were very clever to know how to cross the log and go through the reeds, Ned. And you helped me leap.”

Just then, the most delicious smell of breakfast wafted from their cozy hollow. Warm milk and little fishy treats, all ready and waiting. And there, waiting for them, was Mama Cat, her eyes sparkling with love as she saw them arrive.

“My brave Tilly. My helpful Ned,” Mama Cat purred, wrapping them both in a warm hug. “You are back just in time for a lovely breakfast. I was just about to call you.”

Tilly and Ned settled down happily, Pipkin tucked safely between them on the grey stone. The adventure was over, and everything was warm and bright and happy. As Tilly lapped her warm milk, she remembered her brave leap and how she was not worried about the water near Pipkin this time. Having a friend like Ned, and having Pipkin safe beside her, was the very best thing in the whole wide world. The greatest treasures, it turned out, were the ones you brought safely home.
